web-api-1.pitch: ASP.NET Web API is my go-to for building HTTP/JSON services in .NET.
web-api-1.definition: A .NET framework that maps HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to methods and returns JSON, so any client can use it.
web-api-1.how: Routing matches URL + verb -> model binding fills params -> filters (auth) -> action runs -> formatter returns JSON. Runs on the middleware pipeline with built-in DI.

code.snippet:
[ApiController]
[Route("api/products")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("{id}")]                       // GET api/products/5
    public ActionResult<Product> Get(int id) =>
        _svc.Find(id) is { } p ? Ok(p) : NotFound();  // 200 + JSON, or 404
}
code.note: [HttpGet] maps verb + URL to the method; Ok/NotFound set the status and serialize JSON.

web-api-1.realWorld: At a fintech, one ASP.NET Core API served a React dashboard and an iOS app via versioned /v1 endpoints + JWT; async + caching cut p95 latency ~40%.
web-api-1.when: REST back ends, microservices, SPA and mobile APIs.

diagram.title: ASP.NET Web API request flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Client] -->|HTTP| B[Routing]
  B --> C[Controller / Action]
  C --> D[(Database)]
  C -->|JSON| A

web-api-2.definition: These are three related ASP.NET technologies: Web API builds data services, MVC builds HTML web apps, and ASP.NET Core Web API is the modern, cross-platform successor that unifies both.
keyPoints: ASP.NET Web API: returns data (JSON/XML) for REST services; .NET Framework.
ASP.NET MVC: returns rendered HTML views for browsers; .NET Framework.
ASP.NET Core Web API: cross-platform, faster, merges MVC + Web API on .NET 5+.
Core is the recommended choice for all new development.

web-api-3.definition: Web API is a lightweight framework for RESTful HTTP/JSON services; WCF is a heavier framework for services over many protocols (HTTP, TCP, named pipes, MSMQ) using SOAP and contracts.
keyPoints: Web API: REST-first, HTTP only, JSON, minimal config.
WCF: protocol-flexible (TCP, pipes, MSMQ), SOAP, WS-* standards.
Web API suits the open web and mobile; WCF suits intranet/enterprise.
WCF supports transactions and duplex messaging; Web API does not.

web-api-4.definition: Choosing between them depends on transport and client needs: Web API for open HTTP/REST, WCF for advanced or non-HTTP scenarios.
keyPoints: Web API: public REST APIs, SPA/mobile back ends, microservices.
WCF: TCP/named-pipe/MSMQ transport, SOAP contracts, transactions.
web-api-4.when: Pick Web API for HTTP/REST services on the open web, mobile back ends, microservices and any case where clients are diverse and you want plain JSON over HTTP with minimal setup. Choose WCF only when you specifically need non-HTTP transports (TCP, named pipes, MSMQ), SOAP/WS-* standards, or distributed transactions.

web-api-5.definition: The request lifecycle is the ordered set of stages a request passes through from arrival to response.

diagram.title: Web API request lifecycle
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[HTTP Request] --> B[Hosting / Middleware]
  B --> C[Routing]
  C --> D[Controller Selection]
  D --> E[Model Binding]
  E --> F[Filters]
  F --> G[Action Method]
  G --> H[Formatter]
  H --> I[HTTP Response]

steps: Hosting & middleware receive the HTTP request.
Routing matches the URL and verb to a route.
The controller and action are selected.
Model binding fills the action parameters from the request.
Filters run (authentication, authorization, action).
The action method executes the business logic.
A formatter serializes the result and the HTTP response is returned.

web-api-6.definition: Routing maps an incoming URL and HTTP verb to a specific controller and action, using attribute routes on methods or convention-based templates.

diagram.title: Request routing
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[URL + Verb] --> B[Match Route Template]
  B --> C[Select Controller]
  C --> D[Select Action]
  D --> E[Bind Route Values]

steps: The framework reads the request path and HTTP verb.
It compares them against registered route templates.
It selects the controller and action whose template and verb match.
It extracts route values (like id) from the URL.
It hands off to model binding; if none match it returns 404.

web-api-7.definition: HTTP verbs express the intent of a request, telling the server what action to perform on a resource.
keyPoints: GET: read data (safe, idempotent).
POST: create a new resource.
PUT: replace a resource fully (idempotent).
PATCH: partially update a resource.
DELETE: remove a resource.
HEAD: headers only, no body; OPTIONS: report allowed methods / CORS preflight.
web-api-7.when: Use GET to fetch, POST to create, PUT to fully replace, PATCH to update a few fields, DELETE to remove, HEAD to check existence/headers without a body, and OPTIONS for capability or CORS preflight checks.

web-api-8.definition: HTTP status codes are three-digit numbers that tell the client the outcome of a request: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
keyPoints: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content — success.
400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found.
409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity, 429 Too Many Requests.
500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable — server side.

web-api-9.definition: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for networked APIs built on resources, identified by URLs and manipulated with standard HTTP verbs and representations like JSON.

diagram.title: REST resource interaction
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Client] -->|GET /products| S[Server]
  S -->|200 + JSON| C
  C -->|POST /products| S
  S -->|201 Created| C

keyPoints: Client-server separation.
Statelessness — each request carries all it needs.
Cacheable responses.
Uniform interface (URLs + verbs).
Layered system and resource-based design.
advantages: Stateless design scales horizontally with ease.
disadvantages: Statelessness can mean repeating context (e.g. auth) each call.
Over- or under-fetching is common without careful design.
Strict REST is awkward for non-CRUD actions.

web-api-10.definition: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security mechanism that uses HTTP headers to let a server declare which other origins may call it, relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way.

diagram.title: CORS preflight
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  B[Browser] -->|OPTIONS preflight| S[Server]
  S -->|Allow-Origin / Methods| B
  B -->|Actual request| S
  S -->|Response| B

steps: A browser app on origin A tries to call the API on origin B.
For non-simple requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight.
The server replies with Access-Control-Allow-Origin / Methods / Headers.
If the origin and method are allowed, the browser sends the real request.
Otherwise the browser blocks the response.

web-api-11.definition: You enable CORS in ASP.NET Core by registering a policy and applying it in the middleware pipeline.
steps: In Program.cs call builder.Services.AddCors with a named policy.
In the policy set WithOrigins(...).AllowAnyHeader().AllowAnyMethod().
Call app.UseCors("PolicyName") before MapControllers.
Optionally apply [EnableCors("PolicyName")] per controller or action.

web-api-12.definition: Parameter binding is how Web API fills an action method's parameters from the request: simple types come from the route or query string, complex types come from the request body.
keyPoints: Simple types (int, string) bind from route/query by default.
Complex types bind from the request body.
[FromQuery], [FromRoute], [FromBody], [FromHeader] override the source.
Only one [FromBody] parameter is allowed per action.

web-api-13.definition: Model binding builds complex objects from multiple request sources and validates them; parameter binding is the broader mechanism that also maps simple values.
keyPoints: Parameter binding: the umbrella concept for filling all parameters.
Model binding: its complex-type part, building objects from body/route/query/form.
Model binding integrates with validation via ModelState.
Use [From*] attributes to control binding sources.

web-api-14.definition: Content negotiation is the process where the API and client agree on the response format (JSON, XML, etc.) based on the Accept header and the formatters the server supports.
steps: The client sends an Accept header (e.g. application/json).
The server looks at its registered media-type formatters.
It picks the formatter that best matches the Accept header.
That formatter serializes the response and sets Content-Type.
If nothing matches, it returns 406 Not Acceptable.

web-api-15.definition: Media-type formatters are components that serialize a .NET object to a wire format on the way out and deserialize the body into a .NET object on the way in.
web-api-15.how: On a request, the formatter matching the Content-Type reads the body into an object for model binding. On a response, content negotiation picks a formatter matching the Accept header, which serializes the returned object and sets Content-Type. You register formatters in MVC options and can add custom ones for new media types.

web-api-16.definition: JSON and XML formatters serialize responses to those formats; JSON is the lightweight default for modern APIs, while XML is verbose but still used by some enterprise clients.
keyPoints: JSON: compact, fast, native to JavaScript clients (default).
XML: verbose, larger payloads, supports schemas/namespaces.
You can support both and let content negotiation choose.
web-api-16.how: ASP.NET Core uses JSON by default. Add XML with AddControllers().AddXmlSerializerFormatters(), and tune JSON via AddJsonOptions (casing, nulls). Force a format on an endpoint with [Produces("application/json")]; the default is otherwise driven by content negotiation and formatter order.

web-api-17.definition: Filters run code at specific points in the pipeline to handle cross-cutting concerns without repeating logic in every action.
keyPoints: Authentication filters: establish who the caller is.
Authorization filters: decide whether the caller may proceed.
Action filters: run before/after the action (logging, validation).
Exception filters: catch unhandled errors and shape the response.

web-api-18.definition: The [Authorize] attribute marks controllers or actions as requiring an authenticated (and optionally role- or policy-satisfying) user before the action runs.
web-api-18.how: During authorization the framework checks the ClaimsPrincipal set by authentication. [Authorize] passes if the user is authenticated; [Authorize(Roles="Admin")] or [Authorize(Policy="...")] also evaluate roles or policy requirements. Failing checks return 401 (not authenticated) or 403 (not allowed). Use [AllowAnonymous] to open specific endpoints.

web-api-19.definition: Basic Authentication sends the username and password, Base64-encoded, in the Authorization header on every request.
advantages: Supported by virtually every client and tool.
Good for quick internal tools or testing.
disadvantages: Credentials travel on every request — only safe over HTTPS.
Base64 is encoding, not encryption, so it is trivially decoded.
No expiry or revocation without changing the password.

web-api-20.definition: JWT bearer authentication issues a signed JSON Web Token after login; the client sends it in the Authorization: Bearer header, and the API validates the signature and claims on each request without server-side session state.

diagram.title: JWT authentication flow
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  U[Client] -->|Login credentials| A[Auth Server]
  A -->|Signed JWT| U
  U -->|Bearer JWT| P[Protected API]
  P -->|Validate signature + claims| P
  P -->|200 + data| U

steps: The client logs in with credentials to an auth server.
The auth server returns a signed JWT containing claims.
The client stores the token and sends it as 'Bearer <token>'.
The API validates the signature, expiry and claims on each request.
If valid, the request proceeds; if not, it returns 401.
advantages: Stateless — no server session store, scales well.
Self-contained claims carry identity and roles.
Works cleanly across services and domains.
disadvantages: Tokens cannot be easily revoked before they expire.
A leaked token grants access until expiry.

web-api-21.definition: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework defining how clients obtain access tokens; JWT is just a token format. OAuth often issues JWTs, but they solve different problems.
keyPoints: OAuth 2.0: a protocol/flow for getting and using access tokens.
JWT: a compact, signed token format that can carry claims.
OAuth answers 'how to obtain a token'; JWT answers 'what the token looks like'.
OAuth commonly issues JWTs as its access tokens.
web-api-21.how: In OAuth 2.0 a client runs a flow (authorization code, client credentials, etc.) to get an access token from an authorization server, then calls the API with it. That access token is frequently a JWT, so the two are complementary rather than competing.

web-api-22.definition: API versioning lets an API evolve without breaking existing clients. Common approaches are URL path, query string, header, and media-type versioning.
keyPoints: URL path: /v1/products — explicit and easy to test/cache.
Query string: /products?api-version=1.0.
Header: a custom or Accept header carries the version.
Media-type: version embedded in the content type.
web-api-22.why: I recommend URL-path versioning (/v1/) because it is explicit, easy to test, cache, document and discover, and clients can see exactly which version they call. Header or media-type versioning is a fine alternative when URLs must stay clean, but it is less discoverable.

web-api-23.definition: Exception handling converts errors into proper HTTP responses; global exception handling catches unhandled errors in one place so every error returns a consistent, safe payload.
steps: Add exception-handling middleware early in the pipeline.
It wraps the request and catches any unhandled exception.
It logs the error with context (and a correlation id).
It maps the error to a status code (400/404/500).
It returns a standard ProblemDetails body without leaking internals.

web-api-24.definition: Exception filters handle errors thrown inside the MVC/controller layer with access to the action context; global exception middleware sits earlier and catches errors from anywhere in the pipeline.
keyPoints: Exception filter: controller-aware, fine-grained handling.
Middleware: a true catch-all for the whole pipeline.
Filters miss errors outside MVC; middleware catches them.
Often combined: filters for specifics, middleware as a backstop.

web-api-25.definition: Dependency Injection (DI) is a pattern where a class receives its dependencies from an external container instead of creating them. ASP.NET Core has DI built in and uses it throughout.
web-api-25.why: DI matters because it removes hard-coded 'new' calls, so you can swap implementations (real vs mock), test classes in isolation, and let the framework manage object lifetimes. It is the backbone of clean, maintainable ASP.NET Core apps and is how services like loggers, DbContexts and HttpClients are provided.
advantages: Loose coupling makes code testable and swappable.
disadvantages: Wrong lifetimes cause subtle bugs (captive dependencies).
Indirection can make code harder to follow at first.

web-api-26.definition: You secure a Web API with layered defenses: validate and parameterize input, encode output, use tokens/SameSite cookies, enforce HTTPS and authentication, and apply least privilege.
keyPoints: SQL Injection: use EF Core or parameterized queries; never concatenate input.
XSS: validate and encode output; set a Content-Security-Policy.
CSRF: use anti-forgery tokens or bearer tokens with SameSite cookies.
Always enforce HTTPS, authn/authz, rate limiting and least-privilege DB accounts.
Keep dependencies patched and log security events.

web-api-27.definition: You improve Web API performance by reducing repeated work and payload size and by freeing threads: caching, compression, async I/O, paging and query optimization.
keyPoints: Caching: cache hot data and set HTTP cache headers.
Compression: enable response compression middleware.
Async: make I/O-bound actions async with async/await.
Payload: page, filter and project only needed fields.
Data: add DB indexes and reuse pooled connections; measure before optimizing.

web-api-28.definition: You document and test Web APIs with Swagger/OpenAPI (auto-generated interactive docs) and Postman (crafting, saving and automating requests).
steps: Add Swashbuckle/OpenAPI to generate swagger.json and Swagger UI.
Annotate models, responses and XML comments for richer docs.
In Postman, create a collection and use environment variables for URLs/tokens.
Write test scripts on responses to assert status and body.
Run collections in CI with Newman for automated checks.

web-api-29.definition: You monitor and troubleshoot production APIs with structured logging, centralized aggregation, metrics/health checks, and correlation IDs that tie a single request's logs together.
keyPoints: Structured logging: ILogger/Serilog/NLog writing JSON to a sink (Seq, ELK, App Insights).
Correlation ID: generate or accept one per request and attach it to every log and downstream call.
Health checks and metrics surface problems early with alerts.
Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) follows a request across services.
Avoid logging sensitive data; control log volume and cost.

web-api-30.definition: A high-traffic Web API is designed as stateless, horizontally scalable services behind a load balancer, with token auth, clear versioning, centralized error handling, caching, async I/O and automated deployment.

diagram.title: High-traffic API architecture
diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C[Clients] --> LB[Load Balancer]
  LB --> G[API Gateway / Auth]
  G --> S1[API Instance]
  G --> S2[API Instance]
  S1 --> Cache[(Cache)]
  S1 --> DB[(Database)]
  S2 --> Cache
  S2 --> DB

keyPoints: Architecture: stateless services behind a load balancer + API gateway.
Auth: JWT/OAuth bearer tokens validated at the gateway/service.
Versioning: URL-path (/v1/) so clients upgrade on their own schedule.
Resilience: centralized error handling, retries, rate limiting, circuit breakers.
Performance: caching/CDN, async I/O, paging, tuned queries.
Deployment: CI/CD with health checks, blue-green or rolling releases.
